Lessons.Title: Subtract Your Way
ExplanationParagraphs: Subtract Your Way — Flexible subtraction within 1,000 using pupils' existing place-value strategies.

Source learning goal: Subtract within 1,000 in a way that makes sense to them.. The pupil first explains existing representations; a correct number is not evidence of completing diagrams or partner reasoning.

Warm-up: Number Talk: Subtract Two-Digit Numbers (10 minutes). The independently created companion provides mathematical checks where the 2021 source text explicitly names a computable arithmetic expression; drawing, diagram matching and discussion are teacher reviewed.

Activity 1: Strategies to Subtract (25 minutes). The independently created companion provides mathematical checks where the 2021 source text explicitly names a computable arithmetic expression; drawing, diagram matching and discussion are teacher reviewed.

Activity 2: Base-ten Drawings (10 minutes). The independently created companion provides mathematical checks where the 2021 source text explicitly names a computable arithmetic expression; drawing, diagram matching and discussion are teacher reviewed.
Lesson Synthesis. This teacher-led activity or inaccessible publisher Cool-down is not replaced by an automatic number.
Cool-down: Subtract within 1,000 (5 minutes). This teacher-led activity or inaccessible publisher Cool-down is not replaced by an automatic number.

Start with four mental subtractions. For 428−213 use hundreds, tens and ones to get 215. For 505−398 use counting on from 398 to 505 to get 107, or decompose across a zero. For 394−127 the difference is 267. After pairs construct visual displays, compare number lines, equations and base-ten blocks (MLR7). Activity 2 contrasts Jada and Han: Jada exchanges a ten for ten ones and draws each one; Han partitions and marks a ten without physically redrawing ten individual units. Both depict 262−135=127. Match source diagrams for 252−181=71,262−135=127,252−132=120; image association and pair explanations require teacher review with MLR8. The source calls for actual base-ten blocks and tools for a visual display.

Source numeric expressions verified from indexed 2021 Student Facing HTML: 50 - 10=40; 58 - 10=48; 258 - 20=238; 258 - 24=234; 428 - 213=215; 505 - 398=107; 394 - 127=267; 262 - 135=127; 252 - 181=71; 252 - 132=120. These equations are worked teaching examples; the checker does not include the expected answer in its prompts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Value preserving decomposition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Regrouping base-ten units changes the drawing, not the total.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A hundred equals ten tens, and a ten equals ten ones.

KeyConcepts.Title: Meaning of difference
KeyConcepts.Definition: Subtracting finds what remains or the amount between two numbers.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check that the subtraction matches the story and keep negative intermediate units properly composed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Open source activities
KeyConcepts.Definition: Diagram comparison and discussion require a human judgement.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Correct scalar responses do not establish card or image correspondence.
KeyConcepts.Example: Compare a base-ten drawing that unbundles ten individual ones with one that marks ten partitions directly on the ten; explain why both show 262−135.

WorkedExamples.Title: Count on rather than take away
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 505−398 with a place-value representation.
WorkedExamples.Check: Explain and check the original difference with an addition inverse if appropriate.

WorkedExamples.Title: Exchange one ten to subtract ones
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 262−135 with a place-value representation.
WorkedExamples.Check: Explain and check the original difference with an addition inverse if appropriate.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dropping a composed ten or hundred.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The whole value changes when an exchanged unit disappears.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record all composed place-value units and verify with an inverse operation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Auto-grading a diagram match or explanation using just a number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The public original task requires a representation, explanation and/or partner discourse.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Retain teacher scoring and avoid falsely claimed source image parity.
